Free Silver. A late-nineteenth-century political movement advocating unlimited coinage of silver into money alongside gold, aiming to expand the money supply and aid agrarian and working-class voters. Championed by populists and progressives, it became a central issue in the eighteen ninety-six presidential election, ultimately defeated by the McKinley administration's commitment to gold-only currency.

Free Silver emerged as a response to agricultural depression and the Panic of eighteen ninety-three, when farmers sought currency expansion to raise commodity prices and ease debt burdens caused by deflation. The Panic of eighteen ninety-three crushed agricultural prices and threw millions of Americans out of work, creating urgent political pressure for monetary reform and relief. The movement argued that unlimited coinage of silver into money would inflate the money supply, raise agricultural prices, and redistribute wealth from creditors to debtors, helping farmers pay debts. It appealed especially to farming regions of the South and West, where agricultural depression was most severe and resentment of eastern financial interests was highest. It met fierce opposition from eastern bankers and gold-standard advocates who feared inflation would destabilize the currency and harm financial interests, making investments risky. The debate pitted rural agricultural interests against urban financial interests, creating a sharp sectional divide between America's regions. It was backed by the Populist Party and adopted by William Jennings Bryan as the centerpiece of his eighteen ninety-six Democratic presidential campaign, uniting Democrats and Populists. Bryan's famous Cross of Gold speech in eighteen ninety-six electrified the convention: You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold! This became the iconic phrase of the movement. Free Silver was soundly defeated when William McKinley won the eighteen ninety-six election and committed the nation firmly to the gold standard, ending serious debate over the issue for decades. It symbolized the defeat of agrarian interests in national politics and represented the last major nineteenth-century challenge to gold-standard orthodoxy. Free Silver connects to William Jennings Bryan as the politician who championed it most prominently; the Populist Party as the movement that made free silver central to its platform; the Cross of Gold as Bryan's iconic speech defending the free-silver cause; the Progressive Era as the broader reform era in which free silver was debated; the Panic of eighteen ninety-three as the economic crisis that precipitated the free-silver movement; William McKinley as the politician who defeated free silver and upheld gold; and the American South as a region strongly supporting free silver as a remedy for agricultural depression.
